strengths: The paper proposes a simple and well-motivated alternative to learned compression tokens: selected contextual tokens act as semantic anchors, augmented with an anchor embedding and bidirectional attention. The design is intuitive and technically plausible.

The empirical study covers three compression ratios and 12 MRQA domains, including six out-of-domain datasets. SAC consistently improves average performance over ICAE, 500xCompressor, and EPL, with larger gains at higher compression ratios.
The authors retrain the soft-compression baselines under a common setup and provide useful ablations of bidirectional attention, anchor embeddings, token-selection strategies, and AE/LM objectives.
The results support the narrower claim that SAC can avoid autoencoding pretraining: LM-only SAC outperforms its AE variants while reducing reported pretraining time.
The manuscript is generally clear, and the appendix provides core optimization hyperparameters and per-dataset ablation results.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too narrow for the paper's broad context-compression claims: all experiments use one small model family and size (Llama-3.2-1B) and essentially one task family, extractive QA from MRQA. There is no evidence on larger LLMs, generation, summarization, dialogue, retrieval-augmented generation, or genuinely long-document benchmarks.

Although efficiency is a central motivation, the paper does not report end-to-end inference latency, time-to-first-token, decoding throughput, peak memory, or KV-cache memory. The training-time comparison alone does not establish practical inference benefits, especially because the compressor uses bidirectional attention over the full input.

The strongest 5x results are only modestly above EPL (0.73 F1/0.62 EM in-domain and 0.77 F1/1.00 EM out-of-domain), yet no multiple-seed results, variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided. It is therefore unclear whether these improvements are robust.

Important implementation details are underspecified, including how layerwise anchor KVs are injected into the frozen target model, how attention masks and position IDs are handled, and how positions are assigned when representations from multiple 510-token chunks are concatenated. These choices can materially affect performance and reproducibility.

The novelty is moderate: the method primarily combines representative-token selection, an added token-type embedding, bidirectional encoder attention, and layerwise KV compression, with several ingredients inherited from prior work.

The analysis is largely qualitative. Attention plots are not supported by quantitative measures, and their interpretation is inconsistent: the main text describes SAC as strongly local/diagonal, whereas the appendix characterizes it as sparse and focused on a few key tokens. The t-SNE plots do not establish that distributional proximity causes improved downstream performance.

The comparison to hard compression is limited to LLMLingua-2 and appears potentially mismatched, while the uncompressed Full-FT baseline remains substantially stronger. Additional accuracy-efficiency Pareto comparisons with competitive token pruning, KV compression, and long-context approaches are needed.

The paper overstates conclusions such as avoiding impairment to the model's original language-modeling capabilities; this is not directly evaluated. The claimed anonymous code link is also absent from the supplied manuscript, weakening the reproducibility claim.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and intuitively reasonable idea: use uniformly distributed tokens from the original context as semantic anchors, enrich them with a learned anchor embedding, and let them aggregate information through bidirectional attention.
Across the reported MRQA experiments, SAC consistently improves average F1 and exact match over ICAE, 500xCompressor, and EPL, with larger gains at higher compression ratios.

The component, token-selection, and training-objective ablations provide useful evidence that bidirectional attention, anchor identification, and the language-modeling objective each contribute to performance. The paper also reports training time and includes both in-domain and held-out MRQA datasets.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too narrow to substantiate a general context-compression contribution. It uses only extractive QA tasks from the MRQA collection, one 1B model family, and contexts processed in 510-token chunks. There are no long-document generation, summarization, dialogue, retrieval-augmented generation, or substantially longer-context evaluations.

Although efficiency motivates the work, the paper provides no end-to-end inference latency, time-to-first-token, throughput, or peak-memory measurements. SAC must still encode the uncompressed context with bidirectional attention, so compression ratio alone does not establish practical acceleration. The reported training-time comparison also lacks a token/FLOP-matched accounting across different objectives.

The central comparison is confounded by changing several factors simultaneously: token carriers, anchor embeddings, attention masks, positional layout, and removal of the autoencoding objective. The ablations help but do not include key controls such as passing uniformly selected original tokens directly to the target model, a causal-anchor model under matched compute, or an equal-training-compute comparison of objectives.

The method is underspecified in consequential implementation details, including the exact bidirectional mask, extraction and concatenation of per-layer anchor KVs across chunks, positional IDs assigned to cached KVs and subsequent questions, decoding configuration, dataset sizes and preprocessing, and baseline reproduction settings. No variance across seeds or statistical significance is reported.

The claimed novelty is moderate: uniformly selecting contextual tokens, marking token roles with learned embeddings, and applying bidirectional attention are individually established techniques. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish the combination from token-selection compression and bidirectional LLM encoders at a conceptual level.

The analysis overinterprets qualitative evidence. Proximity in a t-SNE plot does not establish semantic alignment or explain downstream gains, and the attention visualizations lack quantitative measures or controlled examples. Descriptions of the patterns are also inconsistent between the main text and appendix.

Evaluation conventions are unclear. The paper reports “ROUGE-1 F1” for MRQA rather than clearly using the benchmark's standard normalized token-level F1, and it does not document normalization or scoring sufficiently for comparison with prior work.

Several conclusions are stronger than the evidence: experiments do not show that autoencoding generally harms context compression, that language-model capabilities are unimpaired, or that SAC is robust for extreme long-context use. Overall, the consistent gains are promising, but the limited and incompletely specified evaluation is insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: SAC is a clear, technically plausible contribution: selecting contextual anchor tokens, marking them with learned anchor embeddings, and allowing bidirectional encoder attention provides a simple way to avoid context-agnostic compression tokens and autoencoding pretraining.

The evaluation is reasonably broad within MRQA, covering six in-domain and six out-of-domain datasets at 5x, 15x, and 51x compression, with competitive soft- and hard-compression baselines trained under aligned conditions.

SAC consistently achieves the best average F1 and EM. Its advantage over EPL becomes more substantial at higher compression ratios, supporting the claim that semantic anchors are particularly useful under tight information budgets.

The ablations separately examine bidirectional attention, anchor embeddings, token-selection strategies, and AE/LM objectives. They provide useful evidence that both architectural components contribute and that the result is not tied to one sophisticated selector.

Avoiding autoencoding also reduces reported pretraining time by approximately 26% relative to the strongest soft-compression baselines. Hyperparameters and computational resources are documented, and anonymous code is stated to accompany the submission.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrower than the paper's broad claims: all principal experiments use Llama-3.2-1B and MRQA-style question answering. Results on larger models, other model families, summarization, dialogue, retrieval, or genuinely long-document tasks are absent.

The claimed inference-efficiency motivation is not evaluated directly. The paper reports nominal compression ratios and pretraining time but no end-to-end latency, throughput, peak memory, KV-cache size, or compressor overhead. Bidirectional encoding of the full context may be consequential in this comparison.

Contexts are processed independently in 510-token chunks and their compressed representations are concatenated. This weakens the evidence that SAC captures cross-chunk dependencies or solves long-context compression beyond aggregating many short segments.

No multiple-seed results, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. This matters because the improvements over EPL at 5x are modest—about 0.7 F1 and 0.6 EM in-domain, and 0.8 F1 and 1.0 EM out-of-domain.

The novelty is useful but somewhat incremental, combining contextual token selection, a learned token-type embedding, bidirectional attention, and layerwise KV compression. Stronger comparisons isolating these choices against enhanced EPL/500x variants would sharpen attribution.

The representation analysis relies primarily on t-SNE and qualitative attention maps. These visualizations do not establish that distributional proximity causes better task performance, and some interpretations—such as equating local attention with improved information retention—remain speculative.

strengths: SAC presents a clear and practically relevant idea: reuse uniformly selected context tokens as compression anchors, mark them with a learned embedding, and let a bidirectional encoder aggregate context into their layerwise KV representations.

The empirical study is broader than average: it compares against multiple soft-compression baselines on in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA, tests 5x/15x/51x compression, includes 1B/3B/8B models, and adds long-context QA and summarization experiments.

Component, token-selection, and training-objective ablations generally support the architectural choices. SAC consistently improves over the strongest baseline, EPL, especially at 15x and 51x compression.
The paper includes useful efficiency evidence, including theoretical FLOPs, measured compression latency, and training time, and is mostly clear and easy to follow.

weaknesses: The central explanation for why autoencoding is harmful is not convincingly established. Near-zero AE/LM gradient cosine similarity indicates approximate orthogonality, not destructive interference; negative similarity or direct optimization evidence would be needed to support that interpretation. Objective weights and precise sampling/compute matching for the AE+LM comparisons are also insufficiently specified.

The long-context evidence is limited. Summarization compares only with EPL, gains are very small on QMSum (14.95 versus 14.82), no uncertainty or significance analysis is reported, and no uncompressed or strong long-context baseline is provided. Consequently, claims of comprehensive global understanding and broad cross-task generalization are stronger than the evidence.

The scalability claim is overstated. In the full in-domain results, SAC's F1 advantage over EPL falls from 3.43 points at 1B to 1.17 at 3B and only 0.01 at 8B; results also regress on some individual datasets. This contradicts the statement that gains do not diminish with scale.

Efficiency evaluation covers encoder compression latency but not the end-to-end quantities most relevant to deployment, such as time to first token, decoding throughput, peak memory, and total latency across input lengths. Processing long documents as independent 510-token chunks also weakens the claim that anchors integrate information from the entire context.

Several analyses are qualitative or potentially misleading: t-SNE proximity does not establish semantic alignment, attention-map interpretations are based on unspecified examples without aggregate measures, and lower language-modeling perplexity is expected when optimizing only the LM objective.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the manuscript itself: there are no random-seed or variance results, several implementation details of KV injection, position handling, attention masks, objective mixing, and long-context training are underspecified, and the displayed release URL is absent. Overall, the method is promising and technically plausible, but these evidentiary gaps leave it marginally below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The core idea is simple and practically relevant: reusing uniformly selected context tokens as compression carriers, augmented with anchor embeddings and bidirectional encoder attention, avoids introducing separate compression tokens.
The QA evaluation is reasonably broad, covering six in-domain and six out-of-domain MRQA datasets, three compression ratios, and model sizes from 1B to 8B.
SAC consistently improves over the strongest reported soft-compression baseline on average, with particularly clear gains at 15x and 51x compression.
The paper includes useful component, token-selection, and training-objective ablations, as well as preliminary latency, long-context, attention, and representation analyses.
weaknesses: The claimed explanation for removing autoencoding is not convincingly established. Near-zero gradient cosine similarity indicates approximate orthogonality, not destructive interference; no negative cosine or causal evidence is shown. The AE-versus-LM experiments also do not control objective weighting, token exposure, compute, or training duration.

The novelty is moderate. SAC largely combines existing ideas—token selection, EPL-like positional placement, anchor/type embeddings, and bidirectional encoding—without a deeper technical formulation or theoretical result.
The evaluation lacks repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and significance tests. This is important because several headline gains are small, such as the 5x results and the 8B in-domain average.

The practical efficiency claim is under-evaluated. Only compressor latency against 500xCompressor is reported, with unspecified hardware and a roughly 5% gain; there is no end-to-end latency, memory, throughput, prefill/decode breakdown, or comparison with EPL, token-selection methods, and uncompressed inference.

The long-context summarization evidence is weak: only two datasets and one baseline are included, absolute ROUGE scores are low, and no uncompressed model or established long-context method is reported. The 24K QA appendix similarly compares only SAC variants and EPL and omits detailed evaluation settings.

The experimental design does not isolate whether improvements come from semantic anchors, bidirectional attention, the removal of AE, or differences in training compute/data. A particularly important missing control is an EPL-like model trained with LM only under exactly matched compute.

Several interpretations rely on qualitative t-SNE and attention visualizations without quantitative representation or faithfulness measures. t-SNE proximity does not establish that compressed KVs preserve task-relevant semantics.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the reproducibility claim: prompt templates, LoRA target modules, decoding settings, evaluation normalization, random seeds, data mixture details, and hardware for latency measurements are not fully specified.

Some reporting is inconsistent or overstated. Table 6 contains subset averages while the accompanying discussion cites full-dataset averages from later tables; Table 3 initially presents two selected datasets as averages; and claims of strong cross-task generalization exceed the limited non-QA evidence.

The conclusion claims that SAC avoids impairment to the model's original language-modeling capabilities, but the paper does not directly evaluate retained general language-model capabilities or catastrophic forgetting.

strengths: SAC offers a clear and practically relevant approach: it uses selected contextual tokens as semantic anchors, augments them with learned anchor embeddings, and applies bidirectional encoder attention to produce compact KV representations without autoencoding pretraining.

The empirical results are broad and generally convincing. SAC achieves the best average QA performance across 5x, 15x, and 51x compression, improves both in-domain and out-of-domain results, and retains gains when scaling from 1B to 3B and 8B models.

The evaluation includes several strong soft-compression baselines under matched training settings, component ablations, alternative anchor-selection strategies, training-objective ablations, long-context QA and summarization, and theoretical plus empirical efficiency analysis.

Ablations support both principal architectural components: removing bidirectional attention or anchor embeddings consistently lowers average performance. Results also show that sophisticated token selection is not essential, which makes the method comparatively simple and broadly usable.

Avoiding autoencoding reduces pretraining time substantially, while the reported compression latency is lower than that of 500xCompressor. The method therefore has an appealing performance-efficiency trade-off.
The paper is clearly structured, technically plausible, and provides sufficient implementation and hyperparameter details to support reproduction.
weaknesses: The central explanation of why autoencoding hurts is not established rigorously. Near-zero gradient cosine similarity indicates approximate orthogonality, not destructive interference; negative alignment or direct measurements of update interference would be needed to support the stated mechanism.

No results include multiple random seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. This matters because several improvements are small—for example, at 5x compression and on the 8B in-domain average—and SAC loses to EPL on some individual datasets despite broad claims of consistent superiority.

The long-context evidence is comparatively limited: those experiments compare primarily against EPL, omit full-context and stronger hard-compression baselines, and report only a narrow set of metrics. The summarization advantage is modest, especially on QMSum.

The efficiency analysis reports compression-stage latency against only 500xCompressor. It does not provide end-to-end latency, peak memory, decoding throughput, or comparisons with uncompressed inference and other major baselines, so the practical acceleration claim remains incompletely quantified.

The architectural novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental, combining selected original tokens, learned marker embeddings, bidirectional encoding, and an EPL-like positional layout. A simple baseline that directly feeds uniformly selected original tokens to the frozen target model would better isolate the benefit beyond token selection itself.

Some claims are overstated. SAC does not outperform EPL on every individual dataset at all ratios or scales, and the paper claims avoidance of impairment to the language model's original capabilities without directly evaluating general capabilities outside the trained downstream tasks.
